lesson.title: Does This Bell Really Ring True? Checking a Distribution for Normality
lesson.summary: Before applying any rule that assumes a normal distribution, you need evidence that the data actually behave like one, using shape, the empirical rule, and normal probability plots as your checks.
lesson.body:
A remarkable number of statistical tools, from the empirical rule to confidence intervals and hypothesis tests you will meet later, only work correctly when the underlying data are approximately normal. That word approximately matters: real data are never a perfect bell curve, but many datasets are close enough that normal based methods give trustworthy answers, while others are so skewed or lumpy that using those same methods would be a mistake. Assessing normality means gathering evidence, using the histogram and shape vocabulary you already know, before you trust any procedure that assumes a bell shaped distribution.

The first check is visual. Look at a histogram or dotplot of the data and ask whether it is roughly symmetric and unimodal, meaning one clear peak with the two tails tapering off at similar rates. A distribution that is clearly skewed left or right, has two or more separate peaks, or contains extreme outliers is not a good candidate for normal based methods, no matter how convenient that assumption would be. This visual step is quick, but it is also subjective, which is why statisticians pair it with a numeric check.

The empirical rule gives a numeric test. For a truly normal distribution, about 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent fall within two standard deviations, and about 99.7 percent fall within three. Suppose 200 students take an exam with mean 72 and standard deviation 8. If the scores are approximately normal, you would expect about 0.68 times 200, or 136 students, to score between 64 and 80; about 0.95 times 200, or 190 students, to score between 56 and 88; and about 0.997 times 200, or roughly 199 students, to score between 48 and 96. If you count the actual students in each interval and get numbers close to 136, 190, and 199, that is solid evidence the scores are approximately normal. If instead only 150 students fall between 64 and 80, the distribution is probably more spread out or more heavily tailed than a normal curve.

A more precise numeric tool is the normal probability plot, which pairs each observed value with the z-score it would be expected to have if the data were exactly normal, then plots the two against each other. When the data really are approximately normal, the points fall close to a straight diagonal line. Systematic curvature, such as points bending away from the line at both ends, signals skewness, while a small cluster of points far off the line at one end flags an outlier. This tool is more sensitive than eyeballing a histogram, because departures from a straight line show up clearly even in distributions that look roughly bell shaped at a glance.

None of these checks proves a distribution is exactly normal, since real data never are. What they provide is evidence for a judgment call: close enough that normal based methods will give reasonably accurate answers, or different enough that you should use other tools. This judgment becomes essential once you start using the normal distribution to compute areas and probabilities, because every one of those calculations rests on the assumption that the bell curve genuinely describes the data in front of you.
